1.station: On the ridge crest itself, starting from the false summit. Anchors through this stretch are slung blocks and horns; the stations that are actively maintained are recognisable by white-and-black 11 mm static cord, so a station rigged in that cord is the one being looked after.
1.pull: A single 60 m rope covers the ridge rappels. Only about three are needed here because the ground between them is 4th class and gets downclimbed.

2.station: Second of the three crest stations. Parties downclimb 4th-class ridge between stations rather than rappelling continuously, so expect to coil and re-rig.

3.station: Last of the crest rappels; it puts you back at the West Ridge notch, where the descent changes character from ridge to gully.

4.station: The first gully anchor is not at the notch. From the notch you scramble a short way down before reaching a tat station, and that station is the start of roughly six rappels to the base of the gully system.
hazards: The rappel line deliberately avoids the bed of the gully. Dropping into the gully floor to look for anchors puts you in the rockfall funnel that everything above you empties into.
4.pull: 60 m rope from here down; the individual raps are short enough that a doubled 60 m reaches each station.

5.station: The line follows fixed anchors on the small arête alongside the gully rather than in it, which is what keeps it out of the fall line. One station sits on a ledge to the side of the gully and is built from two nuts and two pitons on cord.
hazards: Anything you or the ropes knock loose funnels straight down the gully bed, so keeping yourself and the rope ends on the arête is the whole point of this line
There are several parallel gullies separated by ribs. Late in the season parties use the easternmost one, nearest the deep couloir; picking the wrong one leaves you off the anchor line

10.station: Final rappel lands on snow at the foot of the gully system.
hazards: A large moat has to be crossed to get from rock onto the snow, and it widens as the season goes on. A soloist moving unroped through this section fell about 40 ft into it and broke a leg
Rockfall coming down the gullies above lands in the same place you are standing while you pull the rope
10.pull: Stay tied in for the moat crossing rather than pulling the rope and scrambling it. Parties belay each other across and onto the snow.

1.station: The rappels do not start where you leave the crest. You first traverse well along the southwest (right-hand) side of the ridge to reach a gully. About 200 ft down the gully, on its left-hand side, there is a small tower, and the first anchors sit beside it — a cairn has marked that tower in the past. The alternative to this whole line is downclimbing the loose gully immediately to climber's right of the rappels, which is what parties who cannot find the anchors end up in.
1.pull: 60 m. This one goes as a full rope-stretcher to a big block, or gets split into two shorter rappels if you would rather not run the ends out.

2.station: Rigged on the big block that the first rappel lands at.
hazards: Not every slung boulder on this descent is sound — check what the sling is actually wrapped around before weighting it, because some of the wrapped blocks are suspect
2.pull: Carry plenty of spare cord. Parties routinely strip the worst webbing at each station and add fresh material rather than trusting what is hanging there.

3.station: One of two or three rappels that carry on down toward heather benches.

4.station: Continues down to the heather. Below this station the ropes come off for a downclimb rather than another rappel.

5.station: Picked up after downclimbing through the heather. This station is partly hidden and is the one parties miss.
hazards: Hard to spot from above; walking past it commits you to loose ground with no anchor below

6.station: First of the last two rappels dropping to the col.

7.station: Final rappel onto the Cascade–Johannesburg col.
7.pull: Budget three to five hours for the whole ridge descent — the rappels themselves are the quick part, the traversing and route-finding between them is not.

1.station: West side of the summit. The upper stations are well established and straightforward to find, with a good deal of fixed tat left by earlier parties.
1.pull: Done as full-length rappels on 60 m twins. On a single 70 m rope the same upper ridge takes about five rappels instead.

2.station: Still on established stations. Several of the upper rappels traverse sideways rather than dropping straight down, so you have to work hard in one direction to land on the next anchor.
hazards: The traversing lines make it easy to end up below and off to the side of the next station with no way back up to it
The sideways lines are deliberate — they keep you out of the fall line, so cutting the corner straight down puts you back under loose rock

3.station: Last of the smoothly-linked upper stations before the fixed gear starts thinning out.

4.station: The fixed anchors run out around where a snow gully cuts in on the north side of the ridge — this is the point where some parties abandon the ridge and drop down the south face instead. The next anchor here is an old nest of slings, reached by a rappel of close to 58 m.
hazards: Tat at this station has been found rotten enough to tear apart by hand — inspect and replace rather than clipping what is hanging there
4.pull: Close to a full 60 m. A shorter rope does not reach, and there is nothing obvious in between.

5.station: Continues down; from around here the slings at the following station are usually visible from above.

6.station: Second to last. Keep your head up for stations — they are easy to rappel past on this side of the peak.

7.station: Final rappel onto flat snow at the edge of the glacier. The anchor is slings wrapped around a large block, roughly 15 ft of it, and the rigging can look flimsy enough that parties have backed it up before committing.
hazards: Pulling the ropes here has caught and dislodged blocks onto the party at the bottom — stand out of the fall line and watch the ends come down
A large crevasse sits below the landing. Parties belay each other on the traverse off the snow tongue and on the steep downclimb rather than unroping at the anchor
7.pull: Uses essentially the entire rope to reach flat snow. Crampons on and re-rope for the glacier at the anchor, not afterwards.

1.station: Comes straight off the summit block, rigged around a stack of blocks rather than any fixed gear.
hazards: There is nothing fixed to inspect here — the anchor is whatever you can build out of what is stacked on the summit
1.pull: Double ropes. Parties run on the order of ten 60 m rappels from here down to the glacier.

2.station: Into the upper couloir. The anchors are on the rock walls flanking the couloir rather than in the ice — that is where the first ascent placed pins on the way down, and where later parties still rig. Where the flanking rock gives out, at least one party rappelled off a buried picket.
hazards: This face sheds rock steadily and the couloir is the funnel it all comes down — anchoring on the flanking wall keeps you and the ropes out of the middle of it

10.station: The rappels do not necessarily reach the bottom. Parties commonly stop rappelling partway and downclimb the rest of the couloir, frequently in the dark.
hazards: The bergschrund at the foot of the north-face couloir still has to be crossed to reach the glacier, and it is the last thing you deal with after a long technical descent

1.station: Off the summit block itself, rigged around a stack of blocks rather than fixed gear.
hazards: Nothing fixed to inspect — the anchor is built from what is stacked on top
1.pull: Roughly ten 60 m rappels from here to the snow below, so the descent takes about as long as it sounds.

2.station: Upper couloir. Stations go on the rock walls flanking the couloir rather than in the ice — this is where the first ascent placed pins coming down, and later parties still find or build anchors there. Where the flanking rock is out of reach, a picket buried as a deadman has been used instead.
hazards: The couloir is the funnel for everything the face above sheds; keeping the anchors and the ropes on the flanking wall is what keeps you out of it

10.station: The rappel sequence often does not run all the way out — parties stop rappelling and downclimb the lower couloir where conditions allow, and have finished this in the dark.
hazards: The bergschrund at the foot of the couloir is the last obstacle before the glacier, and you reach it late and tired

1.station: Off the first tower on the ridge.
1.pull: Short — the least demanding of the tower rappels, and the one that sets expectations too low for the three above it.

2.station: Off the second tower into the notch below it.
2.pull: About 40 m, so a single 60 m doubled does not reach. Parties either carry a second line, or rappel as far as one rope allows and then build a second station or belay the last stretch of low fifth class down to the notch.

3.pull: About 40 m again — same problem and same two workarounds if you are on a single rope.

4.pull: Closer to 50 m, the longest of the tower rappels. On one rope this is the one most likely to leave you hanging above the notch.

5.station: Off the top of the Pole of Remoteness. The anchor is a large block on the summit of the tower; parties have tested it deliberately before committing to it.
hazards: Rockfall on this rappel severed a rope on the first ascent. Having a second line in the system is what made that survivable
5.pull: Carry a good length of cord. The single-strand anchors left here have been found in poor shape a year later, and have since been rebuilt redundant — assume you will be replacing rather than clipping.

1.station: The descent is a rappel of the climbing line itself, off the route's own belays, which are almost all bolted and rigged to rappel. Some stations on the buttress are dedicated rappel anchors set off to the side of the climbing belays rather than at them, so the fastest line down is not always straight beneath you. Parties strip down before starting — one dropped everything but two ropes from the top.
hazards: Loose rock remains on the wall and is worse while snow high on the buttress is still melting out
A party below you on the same line is directly under anything you or the ropes dislodge

16.station: The bottom of the wall overhangs. One party lowered their haulbags the final 1,000 to 1,200 ft to the ground in a single continuous lower precisely because the overhanging ground gave them so little to snag on.
hazards: That same overhang cuts the other way on rappel — you can end up hanging free of the rock and needing a swing or a directional placement to reach the next station rather than spinning below it
16.pull: The wall ends in talus above the brushy, mossy slabs at its foot, so the last of the descent is scrambling rather than rappelling.

wa_nooksack_tower_south_face.skip_reason: The South Face is not descended by its own line — parties climb it and go down the north side, so what is published describes the standard north-face descent rather than a set of stations belonging to this route. Beyond a general statement that ten or more rappels may be needed, and one account of a single-rope rappel off a stopper and a runner while trying to reach snow on the west side, no source found describes where any individual station is, what it is built on, or what goes wrong at it. The ten stored stations are an evenly-spaced placeholder sequence rather than a documented line, so there is nothing real to key per-station detail to and any placement would be guesswork.
